paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: a pleasant message isn't the same as a true one. Hananiah told a packed house of priests and people exactly what they wanted to hear, and he said it loud (Jeremiah 28:1-4). Jeremiah even said "Amen!" and wished it were true (Jeremiah 28:6). But Jeremiah wanted good news just like everybody else, and wanting it didn't make it so.

So how do you tell? Jeremiah gave the test: a prophet who prophesies peace is recognized as one the LORD has truly sent only if his word comes true (Jeremiah 28:9). Then the LORD answered, and the answer was heavy. Hananiah broke a yoke of wood, and the LORD said he had fashioned a yoke of iron in its place (Jeremiah 28:13). He had persuaded the people to trust in a lie, and he died that very year (Jeremiah 28:15-17). I think this one is hard to read, and that's okay.

Here's what that means for you, baker. Don't measure a message by how good it feels, because a smooth word that skips what God actually said can leave you worse off than a hard one. Measure it against what the LORD has said, and trust Him even when it's the harder word to hear. The nice-sounding answer might get the applause, but what God says is what you can build on.
